title: Spot the Phish
topicTitle: Phishing hides clues in plain sight
topicBrief: Phishing messages impersonate people or services you trust. Pause before acting: check who sent it, where a link actually leads, and whether the wording is trying to rush you. This is a fictional email inside a safe simulation.
scenario: A suspicious email has arrived in your fictional company inbox. Click the details that do not add up. Every other part is safe to inspect too.

emailContent.subject: Action needed: mailbox storage notice
emailContent.body: Our mail team is performing its normal monthly storage review.
emailContent.urgentPhrase: Your mailbox will be closed today unless you verify it in the next 15 minutes.

clickableRegions.explanation: Nice catch - the real fictional company is Northstar IT, but this sender adds an extra r in the domain.
The subject is ordinary on its own. Check it against other details.
Good eye - a real internal support team would normally address you by name, not a generic greeting.
Exactly - artificial urgency is designed to make you act before you verify the message.
Nice catch - the link preview leads to northstarr-it.thm, not the normal northstar-it.thm site.
A PDF attachment can be normal. It is not a warning sign by itself.
The closing looks polished, but it does not outweigh the sender and link mismatches.

learn.title: Pause, inspect, then decide
learn.body: You found a lookalike sender domain, a generic greeting, pressure to act quickly, and a link that leads somewhere different. These are useful categories to check in any unexpected email: sender spoofing, link mismatches, and urgency language.
